description: HexaByte._06 is a six-member team mapping Earth’s most extreme environments to the future of off-world habitation. By cross-referencing terrestrial geology, climate, and terrain data against lunar and Martian telemetry, we identify high-value planetary analogs to guide permanent base design and astronaut training.
summary:
Finding Mars on Earth compares four Earth locations to Mars to show which best match its conditions. Mars is cold, extremely dry, covered in volcanic rock and salty dust, and has ice underground. No place on Earth matches all of this, so we scored four well-known analog sites on five Mars traits: cold, dryness, geology, ground ice, and special terrain features.
The Antarctic Dry Valleys ranked first (21/25) for extreme cold, dryness, and ground ice. Haughton Crater in the Canadian Arctic followed closely (20/25), offering a real impact crater in a polar desert. Iceland (16/25) and the Atacama Desert (15/25) scored lower overall but each excels at one job: Iceland for basalt rock and lava-tube caves, and the Atacama for ultra-dry, salty, high-UV soil.
The key finding is that no single site is a perfect Mars, so mission teams should match sites to what they are testing. The report includes a ranking chart, a satellite map of the four sites, and a guide to which site suits which test. Scores are based on published descriptions rather than raw satellite data, and future work would compute them from NASA datasets.
details:
What it does: Finding Mars on Earth is a comparison report that identifies which places on Earth are the best practice grounds for Mars missions. Mars is cold, extremely dry, covered in volcanic rock and salty dust, and has ice underground. No Earth site matches all of that, so we scored four well-known analog sites on five Mars traits: cold, dryness, geology, ground ice, and special terrain features. Each trait is scored 1 to 5 and the totals (out of 25) are ranked.
Results: The Antarctic Dry Valleys ranked first (21/25), followed by Haughton Crater in the Canadian Arctic (20/25), Iceland (16/25), and the Atacama Desert (15/25). Each site is also the best match for one specific job: ice drilling and cold-weather gear (Dry Valleys), crater exploration (Haughton), lava-tube and volcanic testing (Iceland), and life-detection instruments in dry, salty soil (Atacama).
Benefits and impact: The report gives mission planners and students a simple, transparent way to see why each site is a good or poor Mars analog, and which site suits which test. The takeaway is that no single site is a perfect Mars, so sites should be matched to what is being tested.
Tools: We used published scientific descriptions of each site and NASA satellite imagery for the map. An AI assistant (Claude) helped organize and draft the report, and Google Drive was used for sharing.
Creativity and factors considered: We chose four sites from different environment types (polar desert, impact crater, volcanic terrain, and hot desert) and built a clear scoring method anyone can check and adjust. We also considered what Earth cannot copy, such as Mars's low gravity and thin air, and we state limitations openly: scores are based on published descriptions, not computed from raw satellite data. Future work would calculate the same traits from NASA Earth and Mars datasets and add an interactive map and Moon targets.
